title: Splice two guardrail panels at a post, lapped in the direction of traffic
instruction: Splice the two grey guardrail panels at the middle post. Stand one on edge against the left and middle posts and the other on edge against the right post, their ends overlapping 3 to 6 cm, centred on the middle post. Lap them in the direction of traffic, which runs the way the white arrows point: at the splice, the end of the panel that traffic reaches first must lie on the road side of (nearer you than) the other panel's end. Then let go of both panels and lift both grippers clear.
context: Highway maintenance workers (O*NET 47-4051.00, whose listed tasks include erecting, installing and repairing guardrails) replace W-beam rail elements after crashes. On strong-post systems the panels are spliced at a post, overlapping about 318 mm (12.5 in, eight splice bolts); newer MGS runs splice mid-span with the same lap rule. Rail elements are lapped in the direction of traffic (Ohio DOT Item 606: 'rail elements shall be lapped in the direction of traffic'; Oregon RD407: 'lap guardrail in direction of adjacent traffic'): at each splice the panel that traffic reaches first lies on the road side of the next one, so a vehicle sliding along the barrier passes over the joint. Lapped the other way, the next panel's end faces oncoming traffic and can snag or spear the vehicle. An inspector reads the lap from one photo of the splice. Here each arm sets the panel on its own side.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm. Five kinds of thing are on the table. (1) Posts: three fixed dark brown painted wood blocks (a timber guardrail post and its blockout as one block), each 25 x 25 mm and 60 mm tall, sides parallel to x and y, centred at x 32.25 cm and y +24.0 cm (left post), 0 (middle post) and -24.0 cm (right post); their road-side (front) faces are in one line at x 31.0 cm, so the middle post covers y -1.25 to +1.25 cm. (2) Road: a fixed dark grey painted board 130 mm (along x) by 700 mm, 2 mm thick, spanning x 12.0-25.0 cm and y -35.0 to +35.0 cm, in front of the posts (between them and the arms). (3) Edge line: a fixed white painted strip 6 mm wide, 700 mm long and 1 mm thick on the road along y, centred at x 24.4 cm. (4) Traffic arrows: three fixed white painted arrows 60 mm long and 1 mm thick on the road, centred at x 18.5 cm and y -10.0, 0 and +10.0 cm, all pointing +y (to the robot's left): traffic runs from the robot's right to its left, so it reaches the right post first. Each arrow is a shaft 10 mm wide along y, from 30 mm on the -y side of the arrow's centre to 25 mm on its +y side, and two head strokes 10 x 25 mm turned 45 degrees either way, touching corner to corner at the tip, 30 mm on the +y side of the centre on the shaft's line (each stroke's centre is 12.4 mm to one side of that line and 5.3 mm short of the tip; the head spans x 16.0-21.0 cm). (5) Rail panels: two loose light grey (galvanised-look) painted pine battens, 300 mm long, 45 mm tall and 18 mm thick, 0.12 kg each, identical and interchangeable. Each stands on a 300 x 18 mm edge with its length along x (pointing away from the robot), centred at x 31.0 cm, one at y +40.0 cm and one at y -40.0 cm: each spans x 16.0-46.0 cm, its broad faces at |y| 39.1 and 40.9 cm. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: End state, read at the last step from the two panels' poses and the two grippers' tool points, finger-tip points and openings. A panel's outline is its box seen from above; at a given y its front edge is the outline's smallest x there (toward the road) and its back edge the largest. Standing: its 45 mm axis within 8 degrees of vertical (either edge down), its lowest point within 3 mm of the table, and still (over the last 0.5 s its centre stayed within 2 mm of where it is and it turned under 2 degrees). The downstream place: a standing panel whose back edge at y +24.0 cm (left post) and at y 0 (middle post) is 0-8 mm in front of the posts' faces (x 31.0 cm; up to 3 mm past them counts, as contact), with its right end (the smallest y of its outline) at y 0 to -5.5 cm. That panel is D, the other U. The shared stretch runs from D's right end to U's left end (its largest y); its length is the overlap (negative if they do not meet). It is read every 2 mm from 5 mm inside each end. Wrong lap: U's left end at most 2 mm short of D's right end or of the middle post's right side (y -1.25 cm), whichever is farther right; U's lowest point within 5 mm of the table; and U's front edge from 1 mm in front of to 15 mm behind D's back edge (behind: farther from the road; U's end is behind D's), at every reading of a stretch of 10 mm or more, else once, U 5 mm inside its left end against D 5 mm inside its right end. Lapped on the road side: U standing, its length within 15 degrees of the y axis, overlap 10-100 mm, and at every reading D's front edge lies from 1 mm in front of to 15 mm behind U's back edge (U's end is in front of D's, on the road side). Released: each gripper's fingers at least 10 mm from both panels' boxes, the fingers taken, whatever their turn, as a cylinder round the gripper's axis from its finger tips 38 mm up, radius hypot(half the finger gap + 10 mm, 20 mm) (60.4 mm wide open); not met on a step when the grippers cannot be read. Score 0 if no panel stands in the downstream place, or if it is a wrong lap. 1.0 if U is lapped on the road side, the overlap is 30-60 mm, the stretch's middle is within 15 mm of y 0 (centred on the middle post), U's back edge at y -24.0 cm (right post) is 1 mm past to 12 mm in front of x 31.0 cm, and both grippers are released. 0.5 if U is lapped on the road side but 1.0 is not met (overlap 10-30 or 60-100 mm, off centre, off the right post, a gripper still on a panel). 0.25 if D is in place and U is neither lapped on the road side nor a wrong lap (U untouched, butted end to end, short of the splice, more than 15 mm in front of D, lying, leaning or lifted, or doubled over D). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. Every outcome takes exactly one of them, checked in this order. The trial ends early once 1.0 has held for 1 s; otherwise it is scored as it stands at the run limit. In a real trial a top photo of the splice shows which end is nearer the road; a tape measures the overlap along the barrier and D's end past the middle post; a feeler gauge or ruler measures the gaps at the posts, the lap gap and the grippers' clearance.
fidelity: About a 1:8 bench model of a strong-post W-beam run: posts 1.905 m apart become 240 mm, the 318 mm lap 30-60 mm. Rigid pine battens stand in for the steel rail; they do not nest or flex, so the lapped panel stands 18 mm proud at the splice, turned about 5 degrees, where real rail nests within its 3 mm of steel. Each panel spans one post spacing, not two; no splice or post bolts. Rigid bodies with the simulator's default friction.
reset_notes: Stand both panels back on edge at their starts, lengths pointing away from the robot, centred at x 31.0 cm and y +40.0 and -40.0 cm. Nothing is consumed; the posts, road and markings are fixed.
